title: Doctrine
html:
Read in the Ide dialect. The original is written in Igbo; here the one term that changes is chi → si, Ide has chi: it is the word, and si / sị is how it is widely said. Nothing here is rewritten — the documents stand as written.

The doctrine of Odiana — Okwu Odiana

What the religion holds: the supreme being, the earth, the personal spirit, the deities, the ancestors, reincarnation, the moral law and the calendar.

Every claim names its source, and where the sources contradict each other the contradiction is stated rather than resolved.

1 · Chukwu — the supreme being

| name | what it is | |---|---| | Chukwu | the supreme God, and the name Odiana uses | | Chineke | the chi that creates | | Chukwu Okike | the creator — the Igbo phrase: "Okike — the Creation aspect of Chukwu" | | Olisabuuwa / Olisabulụụwa | the great Olisa of the world — a form the sources print several ways | | Obasi di n'elu | the Lord above | | Eze Chitoke | king of the creator |

And the tradition builds him no house:

"No shrine is erected directly to Chukwu. No sacrifice is offered to Chukwu. No priest mediates between

the community and Chukwu."

The offering to the supreme being is bloodless, and the sources specify it: "The type of offering made to Chukwu is one made up of kola nut, white chalk and libations of palm and raffia wine" — made "pointing the kola nut to the sun."

This single rule carries the whole religion. The temple has no altar for blood because the tradition never built one for the high God; the offering is oji, nzu and mmanya because that is what the tradition offers; and there is no mediator because the tradition has none.

2 · The order of the divine

Four kinds, and the sources keep them apart:

| | is | |---|---| | Chukwu | the supreme being — no shrine, no sacrifice, no mediator | | the alusi | a class of its own: "neither living human beings (mmadụ) nor dead human beings (mmụọ)" | | the ancestors | ndị ichie, ndị mmụọ — "the Unseen Seen" | | chi | one to each person — not a god to be worshipped, but a relationship to be kept |

Odiana does not rank them. the old order centralised by assigning functions, not by ordering the divine, and Odiana does the same: each power has a work, and no council rules on which is senior — except in §3, where the tradition itself argues the question.

3 · Ana — the earth, and the argument about her

Ana is the earth, and she is the centre of the moral order. She records every deed; she is the enforcer of the law; she is the ground that receives the dead. Odiana's whole law rests on her — law is Ana.

And the sources argue about how far that goes

  • One scholar: "If ever there was a supreme god among the Igbo, it was Ana."
  • Field informants, asked which is greater: "We are constrained to declare that Ana is greater,

this Ana on which our feet rest."

  • And a verse: "Chukwu created Ana and mankind / but Ana is greater."
  • Another scholar, answering: "a strong doubt that the Igbo regard Ana as a single universal

deity … it is more likely a generic name … each community has its own Ana."

  • And fieldwork: "they said it was the local Ana and not some general conception of the land."
  • And the source's own verdict: "Ana is not a single universal deity. Being local, she cannot

logically be supreme."

Odiana's position — the two claims separated

Odiana holds the first and declines the second:

Ana is the greatest of the powers and the ground of the law. She is present as a particular earth in

each place. One dignity, many Ana.

That is not a compromise between scholars — it is how the cult already works, with one shrine of the earth per community, all of them Ana — and it takes the claim that is attested twice independently while leaving the one the best evidence contradicts.

A naming note. Central Igbo writes Ana; the Igbo form is Ana/Ani, and the old order's earth priest is the eze ana. Odiana writes Ana in its own voice and keeps Ana/Ani inside the the old order names, which is why the priest is eze ana and not eze ana.

4 · chi — the personal spirit

chi is one to a person — a fragment of the supreme light placed in every human being. It is not a guardian angel and not a god: it is the person's own spirit, and the relationship with it is kept, not worshipped.

| the doctrine | | |---|---| | the alignment | the attested form is onye kwe chi ya ekwe — when a person agrees, their chi agrees | | the negatives | chi ọjọọ — a hard or ill-fated chi — is attested | | the limit | a diviner may do great things, "but when it comes to one's destiny… you are the only one that can save yourself" | | the keeping | the chi is addressed daily at the household altar, Obi Chi, which "can be as simple as an altar" | | the cult is women's | the chi feast in the tradition is a women's feast, and a woman's chi altar is a small water-filled vessel — one more reason the Iyi is a head and not a helper | | the enemies | greed, pride and fear — the three the tradition names as what deafens a person to their own chi |

5 · The ancestors, and the spirit-land

The dead are not erased. "The ancestors are not dead; they are the Unseen Seen. They are the roots of the living tree."

Ana mmụọ, the spirit-land, is "a mirror of the world, but reversed" — the sun sets where ours rises, rivers flow upward — and it has three territories: the council-hut of the elders, where the great ancestors sit and guide the living; the periphery of mists, where those whose wrongs are unresolved wait; and the forest of rebirth, where souls ready to return gather.

And judgement is not vengeance. The soul comes before a council of elders and places its ofo before them — "the ofo is the witness of the life that was lived; it is not weighed against gold, stone, feather or any other object." They ask:

"What did you do? What did you owe? What did you leave behind?"

One who recognised their wrongs and repaired what they could finds their ofo light; one who seemed righteous while living through deceit finds it burdened. "Ana does not count appearances; Ana reveals consequences."

And the ancestors are honoured with nothing killed. The sources record a cult of the dead in which "there is no sacrifice made" to the skulls venerated, "yet they still impose a long-term responsibility on society." That is the doctrinal warrant for a bloodless ancestor cult — not a subtraction from the rite, but a form the rite already takes.

6 · Reincarnation — ilo uwa

"Reincarnation is not a possibility; it is a covenant sealed by the soil."

The gateway is the burial. Without the rite of the seven clods performed by a rightful elder over a body laid in ancestral ground, the soul is barred from returning and wanders the mists until a descendant performs the corrective burial. The body is washed with clean water, wrapped in white, and the grave faces east.

And the return is graded by how a life was lived:

| | | |---|---| | one who dies defending their people | returns within a single generation | | a coward or a betrayer | waits many generations | | a child who dies at birth | returns immediately, to the same mother |

ebibi — the tradition's own theory of justice

And the doctrine does not stop at rebirth. The Igbo world is conceived in market terms — "guaranteeing only equality of opportunity but not equality of outcome" — and standing can be renegotiated:

"He can still negotiate a more rewarding social status for himself during the next cycle of reincarnation

through the institution of ebibi."

So the judgement of Odiana is neither final nor merely punitive: it is a market with another round. That is the tradition's own answer to why the wicked prosper, and it is more forgiving than most religions' answers.

7 · The alusi

| power | governs | |---|---| | Ana | the earth, law, morality, the dead — §3, the centre of the moral order | | chi | personal destiny — §4 | | Anyanwu | the sun; the witness of truth, the opener of the day. Graves face east towards him, and the morning rite and the nzu sun-bath are his | | Onwa | the moon; time, rhythm, return | | Idemili | sacred water, and the python. "She carried purity and danger together" | | Amadioha | thunder and lightning — "the voice of cosmic justice". The law of restitution is his | | Agwu | knowledge, intuition, divination and creativity. The trickster — and the doctrine is "Agwu reveals through afa", not that afa is Agwu | | Ikenga | personal force and achievement; the right hand | | Njoku | the soil; patience and sustenance. Mmaji, his counterpart, is "the yam's knife" — the tool that divides | | Ekwensu | see below | | Ogbanje | children who come and go |

Ekwensu — and the rule that follows

The name carries four incompatible senses in the sources: a power of war; a tester of intention at the boundaries; the devil; and — in a the old order classification of the dead — "lived a short span, died accidentally and cannot reincarnate", which is a status of the departed and not a god at all.

And the tradition rejects the devil reading outright: "Far from being a devil figure, Ekwensu is the universal chi that resists evil."

So Odiana uses no name without saying which sense it means, and it does not carry the Christian devil into an Igbo word.

8 · The moral law

| term | is | |---|---| | omenala / omenani | the custom, the way of the land — one etymology is "it happened on Ani" | | iwu | enacted law, made by a head and a council; breach is punished or fined | | nso | taboo — inherited, not made by anyone; breach brings defilement | | alu | abomination — the one word for it. arụ is not kept as a second term; where a source uses it of a body, that is the body, and not an abomination | | ikpu alu | the cleansing of abomination | | isube nso | the promulgation, and the abrogation, of taboo | | nsọ Anị | the crime-term: what is taboo in the world of the earth |

iwu is not nso, and this is the hinge of the religion. "The the old head and his councils make laws to be obeyed by the whole of the old order. An infraction of these laws does not constitute breaking a taboo." So Odiana legislates by iwu, never by pretending a new rule is an old taboo.

The offences and the remedies

| offence | remedy | |---|---| | theft | restitution fourfold | | injury | not retaliation — the offender works the victim's farm for a full planting season | | murder | not death — banishment and the blood-price to the family | | moving a sacred boundary stone | the stone returned and the wound sealed | | incest | the union is a lost echo: it cannot inherit, nor live on the land | | a false oath on the ofo | banishment until public confession | | poverty | alu — "Poverty is disorder, not virtue." |

And the law restores rather than avenges. "Justice is not about revenge; it is about restoring the broken circle of the community." Even of the dead: "judgement is not vengeance."

And the guilt is shared — the heaviest doctrine in the religion: "When someone commits nso, it affects the whole community; and if the crime is severe enough, entire groups and everyone would be held responsible." That is why the remedy is public, and why a communal guilt needs a cleansing a whole community can perform.

9 · The calendar

The week is four days — Eke, Orie, Afo, Nkwo — and the days are persons, not numbers. The year counts thirteen moons, and the intercalary day is the author's to set.

The calendar is announced, not computed locally: the Nzemabua publishes it in Igu Aro, and no Ndose sets its own. The tradition computes the festival dates from lunations.

And the year is gendered: the the old order ritual calendar carries "OFFERING TO MEN'S CHI" and "OFFERING TO WOMEN'S CHI" as separate entries — the calendar warrant for the dual headship of constitution.md §2.

10 · What Odiana does not teach

  • No devil. Ekwensu is not Satan, and no Igbo word is made to carry him.
  • No hell. The periphery of mists is "a homestead, not a prison", and even it is correctable.
  • No eternal punishment. ebibi gives the wrongdoer another round.
  • No mediator. No priest stands between a person and Chukwu.
  • No blood to the supreme being — the tradition never offered any.
  • No shrine to Chukwu — and therefore no altar in Odiana for blood to fall on.
  • No borrowed furniture. No chakras, no Akashic Records, no power animals, no master numbers, no third

eye, no zodiac, no energy field, no universe as an agency. And no Christian overlay: no sin in the Christian sense, no grace, no salvation, no sacrament.

The blood ruling, in one place

(The ruling is canon.md A11, and it is the same in every document of this religion.)

An animal is killed at every festival of Odiana and at every serious rite of it. The announcing of the year, the cleansing of a great abomination, the taking of a title, the consecration of a Dibia, the setting of a boundary, the burial of a head, the making of peace, and the opening of a war. The animal is killed in the open, and its blood is spilled upon open ground, away from every holy thing.

And no blood is brought to a shrine, or to an altar, or to a sacred object, or to a tree that is held sacred. Nothing holy in this religion is ever touched with blood. The altar keeps the kola, and the nzu, and the wine, and the water. This is a modernisation of Odinana and it is iwu — made, and published, and dated — and it is not a custom recovered from the ancestors.

What remains bloodless, and stays bloodless:

  • the offering to Chukwu — the tradition's own offering was kola, white chalk and libation, and it is kept;
  • the household shrine — the household oblation is kola, nzu, mmanya and water;
  • the temple altar — no blood is brought to it, ever;
  • the consecration of objects — no shrine, Ofo, Ikenga or medicine is made with blood (canon.md A6);
  • a reading of afa — the reading is free: nothing is charged for it, and the offering is not a fee.

And the one blood that is never shed in this religion, in any rite and for any purpose, is human blood. Where the old practice used a human being, this religion uses the fowl — for it is the fowl that is used in performing sacrifice, and not a human being.
